en: The Sutra of the Buddha’s Brief Instruction on the Teaching Just Before His Parinirvāṇa, also titled the Sutra of the Bequeathed Teaching.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Kumārajīva of Kucha during the Later Qin Dynasty under imperial decree.

When Śākyamuni Buddha first turned the wheel of Dharma, he delivered Ājñātakauṇḍinya; finally, when preaching the Dharma, he delivered Subhadra. Those who were to be delivered have all been delivered, and he is now about to enter parinirvāṇa between the twin śāla trees.
At that time, during the silence of midnight, he briefly expounded the essential Dharma to his disciples:
"O bhikṣus, after my parinirvāṇa, you should revere, treasure, and honor the Prātimokṣa, as if those in darkness encountered light, or as a poor man obtained a treasure."
You should know that this person is your true teacher; he is no different from me were I to remain in the world.

Those who uphold the pure precepts must not engage in buying and selling, nor establish fields and houses, nor keep people as servants or slaves, nor raise livestock. All forms of cultivation and all kinds of wealth and treasures should be avoided at all times, as one would avoid a pit of fire.

One must not cut down trees or grass, nor plow the soil or dig the earth; one should not compound medicinal decoctions, practice divination for good or ill fortune, gaze upward at the stars and constellations to calculate their waxing and waning, or engage in calendrical computations and arithmetic—all such activities are improper.

One should restrain the body, eat at the proper times, and maintain a pure livelihood; one must not involve oneself in worldly affairs or act as a messenger, nor should one practice incantations or elixirs, nor cultivate intimacy with the noble or engage in familiar and disrespectful behavior—none of these should be done.
One should straighten one's own mind and seek deliverance through right mindfulness; one must not conceal faults or display eccentricities to delude the multitude.
Regarding the four types of offerings, one should know moderation and contentment; whatever provisions are obtained for service should not be accumulated.
This is a brief explanation of the characteristics of upholding the precepts.
Since the precepts are the foundation for correctly conforming to liberation, they are called *prātimokṣa*.
By relying on these precepts, one attains various meditative concentrations (*dhyāna-samādhi*) as well as the wisdom that extinguishes suffering.
Therefore, bhikṣus, you should maintain the pure precepts and not allow them to be violated.
If a person can maintain the pure precepts, they will be able to possess wholesome dharmas;
if there are no pure precepts, none of the various wholesome merits can arise.
Therefore, you should know that the precepts are the foremost dwelling place for the merit of peace and security.

"You bhikṣus, having already been able to abide in the precepts, must now restrain the five sense faculties so that they do not become heedless and enter into the five desires. It is like a cowherd who holds his staff and watches over his herd, not allowing them to run wild and trample upon the crops."

If one放任 the five sense faculties, not only will the five desires become boundless and impossible to restrain, but it will be like an unruly horse that, if not controlled by a bridle, will drag its rider down into a pitfall.

While the suffering of being robbed or harmed lasts but a single lifetime, the calamity of the thieves of the five sense faculties extends to successive generations; their harm is exceedingly grave, and one must not fail to be cautious.
Therefore, the wise person restrains them rather than following them, holding them as one would a thief so they do not run wild;
even if one were to let them loose, they will all soon be seen to perish.
Of these five faculties, the mind is their master.

Therefore, you should well restrain the mind; the mind is more fearsome than venomous snakes, evil beasts, or hostile robbers, and even a great, overflowing conflagration is insufficient to serve as a metaphor for it.

Fickle and restless in its movements, it sees only the honey and not the deep pit; like a mad elephant without a hook or a monkey that has found a tree, it bounds and leaps about, difficult to restrain. One must quickly subdue it so that it does not become heedless.
"To let this mind run wild is to lose all that is good for a person; to restrain it in one place, there is nothing that cannot be accomplished.
Therefore, bhikṣus, you should be diligent and energetic in subduing your minds."

“O bhikṣus, when you receive various foods and drinks, you should regard them as taking medicine; whether they be good or bad, do not give rise to feelings of preference or aversion, but accept them merely to sustain the body and eliminate hunger and thirst.”
Just as a bee gathers from flowers, taking only their nectar without damaging their color or fragrance;
so it is with a bhikṣu: he accepts the offerings of others only to take what removes his own afflictions, and must not seek much, lest he ruin his virtuous mind.
It is like a wise person who gauges the strength of an ox to determine how much it can bear, not overexerting it so as to exhaust its power.

"You bhikṣus, during the day you should diligently cultivate wholesome dharmas and not let the time pass in vain; during the first and last watches of the night, do not neglect your practice either. In the middle watch of the night, recite the sūtras to refresh yourselves, lest you allow sleep to cause this entire life to pass empty-handed without attainment."
One should reflect that the fire of impermanence burns all worlds; seek early deliverance for yourself and do not sleep.
The thieves of the various afflictions constantly lie in wait to kill one, even more so than an enemy; how can you sleep soundly without being startled awake?
The venomous snake of affliction sleeps within your heart; it is like a black viper sleeping in your room. You must use the hook of moral discipline to expel it early.
Only when the sleeping snake has been driven out can you sleep in peace; to sleep while it remains is to be a person devoid of shame.
The garment of shame is the foremost among all forms of adornment; shame is like an iron hook, capable of restraining a person from what is unrighteous.
Therefore, bhikṣus, you should always maintain a sense of shame and never allow it to lapse for even a moment;
if you abandon shame, you will lose all meritorious qualities.
Those who possess a sense of shame possess wholesome dharmas;
those without shame are no different from the birds and beasts.

"O bhikṣus, if someone should come and sever your limbs one by one, you should restrain your own minds and not give way to anger or resentment, and you should also guard your speech so that no evil words issue forth."
If one gives rein to a mind of anger, one will obstruct one's own path and lose the benefits of merit.
As for the virtue of patience, it is something that neither the observance of precepts nor ascetic practices can equal.
Only those who are able to practice patience may be called powerful great beings.
If one cannot joyfully endure the poison of foul abuse as if drinking nectar, they are not called a person of wisdom who has entered the Way. Why is this so?
The harm of anger can destroy all wholesome dharmas and ruin one’s good reputation; in both this life and future lives, people take no pleasure in seeing it.
You should know that a mind of anger is more fierce than a raging fire; you must always guard against it so that it does not gain entry, for there is no thief of merit greater than anger.
Laypeople who indulge in desires and do not practice the Way lack the means to self-restrain themselves; thus, their anger may still be excused.
However, for those who have left the household life to practice the Way and are free from desire, to harbor hatred and resentment is utterly unacceptable.
"It is as if lightning were to strike and ignite a fire within clear, cool clouds; it is utterly incongruous.

You bhikṣus, you should touch your own heads: you have already cast off ornaments and donned dyed robes, and you carry alms-bowls to sustain yourselves through begging. Seeing yourselves thus, if pride should arise, you must extinguish it quickly."

To harbor such arrogance is inappropriate even for a layperson in the secular world; how much more so for one who has left the home life to enter the Path, begging for alms while having subdued their own mind for the sake of liberation?
“O bhikṣus, a crooked and deceitful mind is contrary to the Path; therefore, you should make your minds upright and honest.
You should know that crookedness and deceit serve only for deception, and have no place for one who enters the Path.”
Therefore, you should straighten your minds, taking integrity as your foundation.
"O bhikṣus, you should know that those with many desires suffer much affliction because they seek many gains;
those with few desires have no seeking and no desire, and thus lack these troubles."
One should practice even the mere state of having few desires; how much more so since having few desires can give rise to all manner of wholesome merits?
A person with few desires has no flattery or crookedness to seek the favor of others, nor are they led astray by the sensory faculties.
One who practices few desires has a mind that is tranquil, free from anxiety or fear; in all matters they have abundance and are never lacking. Where there is fewness of desire, there is Nirvana.
This is called having few desires.
"O bhikṣus, if you wish to be liberated from all suffering and affliction, you should contemplate contentment; the dharma of contentment is itself the place of wealth, joy, and peace."
One who is content is peaceful and happy even when lying upon the ground;
one who lacks contentment finds no satisfaction even when dwelling in heaven.
The discontented are poor despite their wealth; those who are content are rich despite their poverty.
Those who lack contentment are constantly led astray by the five desires and are objects of pity for those who possess contentment;
this is called "contentment.

"O bhikṣus, if you seek the peace and bliss of the unconditioned (asaṃskṛta), you should leave behind clamor and dwell alone in seclusion. Those who dwell in such quietude are held in common reverence by Śakra and the various devas."
Therefore, one should abandon both one's own group and other groups, dwelling alone in seclusion to contemplate the eradication of the root of suffering.
Those who delight in crowds will undergo manifold afflictions; it is like a great tree upon which many birds gather, which then faces the calamity of withering and breaking.
The world is bound by attachments and submerged in manifold sufferings, like an old elephant mired in mud, unable to extricate itself.
This is called "detachment.

"O bhikṣus, if you apply yourselves with diligent vigor, then no task will be difficult. Therefore, you should be diligent and vigorous; just as a small stream, if it flows constantly, can pierce through rock."

If the mind of the practitioner repeatedly succumbs to indolence and desists— just as one who drills for fire stops before it has grown hot, making it difficult to obtain fire despite his desire for it—
this is called diligence.
“O bhikṣus, you should seek out virtuous friends and seek virtuous protection and assistance, and never forgetful of mindfulness;
for if you do not forgetful of mindfulness, the thieves of the afflictions will be unable to enter.”
Therefore, you should always maintain mindfulness within your hearts; if you lose mindfulness, you will lose all merits.

If the power of your mindfulness is firm and strong, even if you enter among the bandits of the five desires, you will not be harmed by them, just as one who enters battle wearing armor has nothing to fear.
This is called non-forgetfulness of mindfulness.

"O bhikṣus, if you restrain the mind, the mind will abide in samādhi; because the mind abides in samādhi, you will be able to know the characteristics of the arising and ceasing of phenomena in the world."

Therefore, you should always diligently cultivate and accumulate various concentrations. If one attains concentration, the mind will not be distracted; it is like a household that cherishes water and skillfully maintains its dikes and ponds.
The practitioner is likewise: for the sake of the water of wisdom, they skillfully cultivate meditative concentration so that it does not leak away.
This is called concentration.

"O bhikṣus, if you possess wisdom, you will be free from greedy attachment; by constantly examining yourselves, do not allow yourselves to fail. In this way, you shall attain liberation within my Dharma.
If it is not so, you are neither a man of the Way nor a layman; you have no name at all."

True wisdom is the sturdy ship that carries one across the ocean of old age, sickness, and death; it is the great bright lamp in the darkness of ignorance; it is the excellent medicine for all suffering and illness; and it is the sharp axe for those who would fell the tree of afflictions.
Therefore, you all should increase your own merit through the wisdoms of hearing, reflection, and cultivation;
for if a person possesses the illumination of wisdom, they see clearly even without the divine eye.
This is what constitutes wisdom.
"O bhikṣus, if you engage in various forms of conceptual proliferation, your minds will become distracted; even though you have left the household life, you have not yet attained liberation."
Therefore, bhikṣus, you should urgently abandon the distracted mind and frivolous proliferation;
if you desire to attain the bliss of tranquility, you must skillfully extinguish the affliction of frivolous proliferation.
This is called non-proliferation.
"O bhikṣus, you should always be single-minded regarding all meritorious qualities, abandoning all negligence as you would avoid a hostile thief."
The Greatly Compassionate World-Honored One has brought all that you desire for your benefit to ultimate fulfillment; you should simply practice it with diligence.

Whether in the mountain ranges, in empty marshes, beneath trees, or in secluded rooms, keep in mind the Dharma you have received so as not to let it be forgotten. You must always encourage yourselves and cultivate it with vigor, lest you die in vain and later fall into sorrow and regret.
I am like a skilled physician who diagnoses the illness and prescribes the medicine; whether it is taken or not is not the fault of the physician.
Again, I am like a good guide who leads others onto the path of goodness; that they hear it but do not act upon it is not the error of the guide.
"If you have any doubts regarding the Four Noble Truths, such as suffering and the rest, you may ask about them quickly; do not harbor uncertainty without seeking a resolution.
At that time, the World-Honored One made this proclamation three times, yet no one asked a question.
Why is this? Because the assembly is free from doubt.
At that time, Anuruddha, observing the minds of the assembly, addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
The moon might be made hot, and the sun might be made cold, but that which the Buddha has taught as the Four Noble Truths cannot be made otherwise.
The Truth of Suffering taught by the Buddha is truly suffering; it cannot be made into pleasure.”
The arising of suffering is the true cause, and there is no other cause;
if suffering is extinguished, it is because the cause has been extinguished, and because the cause is extinguished, the fruit is extinguished.
The path for extinguishing suffering is the true path, and there is no other path.
“World-Honored One!
These bhikṣus have attained certainty and are free from doubt regarding the Four Noble Truths.

Among this assembly, those who have not yet completed their tasks will feel sorrow at the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa; yet those who have newly entered the Dharma shall all attain deliverance upon hearing what the Buddha has spoken, just as one who sees a flash of lightning at night can immediately perceive the path.”
"Those who have already accomplished what was to be done and have already crossed the ocean of suffering merely think:
'How swift is the passing into parinirvāṇa of the World-Honored One!
Although Ānanda spoke these words, everyone in the assembly had fully realized the meaning of the Four Noble Truths.
The World-Honored One, wishing to cause this great assembly to all attain firmness, again preached for the sake of the multitude out of his heart of great compassion:
"You bhikṣus, do not harbor grief or distress."
If I were to remain in the world for an eon, my assembly would still eventually perish; for those who have gathered, it is ultimately impossible not to part.
Since I am fully endowed with the Dharma that benefits both myself and others, my remaining longer would provide no further benefit.
Those who were to be saved—whether in the heavens or among humans—have all already been saved; and as for those not yet saved, the causes and conditions for their salvation have all been established.
From this day forward, my disciples shall transmit and practice this in succession; thus, the Dharma-body of the Tathāgata will remain eternally present and never perish.
Therefore, you should know that all things in the world are impermanent; where there is meeting, there must be separation. Do not harbor grief.
Such is the nature of the world; you should apply yourself with diligent effort to seek liberation early, using the light of wisdom to extinguish the darkness of ignorance.
The world is truly precarious and fragile, possessing nothing that is firm or enduring; my present attainment of extinction is like being cured of a malignant disease.

This is a sinful thing that ought to be abandoned, a mere provisional designation for what is called a "body," submerged in the great ocean of birth, old age, sickness, and death. What wise person, having attained its eradication, would not rejoice, as if slaying a hostile enemy?
“O bhikṣus, you should always single-mindedly and diligently seek the way out. All phenomena in the world, whether conditioned or unconditioned, are characterized by decay and lack of security.”
"Cease, all of you, and do not speak further; the time is nearly past and I am about to enter parinirvāṇa. This is my final instruction.
*The Sutra of Brief Exhortations Spoken by the Buddha as He Was About to Enter Parinirvāṇa*
